droplet.overview: In this droplet, we continue our journey in building Wolly's Mobile app using SwiftUI. We'll focus on designing the ItemDetails screen, implementing functionality to add items to the cart, and creating a Cart page to display all items present in the cart. Additionally, we'll explore techniques to define data, abstract work, and reduce duplication in our app. By connecting design and data, we aim to create a responsive and seamless user experience.

prerequisites.name: Building Your First App (Wolly's Mobile)
prerequisites.description: In this droplet, we'll begin by constructing the fundamental elements of Wolly's mobile app. Subsequently, we'll organize these elements using Stacks and optimize the code to incorporate Reusable components. Finally, we'll delve into navigation functionalities within SwiftUI.
learningObjectives: Be proficient in using SwiftUI components such as Stacks
Organize code using Subviews and Lists

blocks.content:
In the previous droplet, we began constructing Wolly's Mobile app by setting up the initial project in Xcode and familiarizing ourselves with SwiftUI's fundamental concepts. We explored using Stacks for structuring UI elements, creating lists and subviews for organizing content and implementing basic navigation functionalities using NavigationStack and NavigationLink.

In this droplet, we will focus on designing the ItemDetails screen, implementing functionality to add items to the cart, and creating a Cart page to display all items present in the cart. Additionally, we will explore techniques to define data, abstract work, and reduce duplication in our app. Finally, we will connect our design and data together to create a responsive and seamless user experience.

In the previous droplet, we created a struct WollyItem in ContentView which looked like this -

struct WollyItem: Identifiable {
    var id = UUID()
    var title: String
    var imageName: String = "tag.fill"
    var price: Double
}

This represents each item available on the app. We are storing the item properties such as id, title, imageName and price. It conforms to the Identifiable protocol, which requires a unique identifier for each item. We also default the imageName to the value tag.fill.

Now, let's enhance our code architecture by relocating the WollyItem struct to its dedicated file, named WollyItem.swift. To do this click on File → New → File… → Swift File and name it as WollyITem. Then remove the struct WollyItem from ContentView and add it to this file. This separation promotes better organization, modularity, and reusability within our project. With this improved structure, we can effortlessly import the WollyItem struct across different components of our application, maintaining a cleaner and more maintainable codebase.

This is how the WollyItem swift file should look like.

This is how the ContentView should look like at this point.

In the previous droplet, we also added a struct named Examples that contained an array of WollyItems of the type WollyItem.

To improve the Examples struct, let's create a dedicated Examples swift file. Within this file, we'll create static instances of all WollyItems, making them easily accessible throughout the project. By centralizing this instantiation in its own file, we improve code management and ensure consistent access to example data. This organization enhances code clarity, promotes reusability, and simplifies maintenance, leading to a more streamlined and scalable project structure. Additionally, isolating the examples improves readability and reduces the clutter in the main file, resulting in a cleaner and more modular codebase.

Let’s create the Examples file by clicking on File → New → File… → Swift File and naming the file as Examples.

Next, let’s remove the struct Examples from ContentView and move it to the file we just created. At this point, the code in ContentView would look like this -

The Examples file should look like this -

Now let us change the Examples struct to define static instances of each WollyItem. This modification significantly enhances the readability and maintainability of the codebase. By explicitly naming and defining each WollyItem within the Examples struct, developers can easily comprehend and access individual items. Moreover, this approach improves accessibility, enabling direct usage of specific items in various parts of the project without the need for manual instantiation.

// Represents Examples of WollyItems
struct Examples {

	// static instances of each item 
  // Great if we want to preview a single item (DetailView, ListRowView, etc.)
  static let muffin = WollyItem(
      title: "French Toast Muffin", price: 2.5)
  static let coffee = WollyItem(
      title: "Iced Coffee", price: 4.49)
  static let bagel = WollyItem(
      title: "Bagel", price: 1.65)
  static let cookie = WollyItem(
      title: "Cookie", price: 1.99)
  static let brownie = WollyItem(
      title: "Brownie", price: 1.8)
  
  // static list of many items
	// great for sampling a whole group (cart, list, etc.)
  static let wollyItems = [muffin, coffee,
                           bagel, cookie, 
													 brownie]
}

The static list of wollyItems serves as a comprehensive collection for sampling groups of items, facilitating tasks such as populating shopping carts or displaying product lists. Centralizing the instantiation of WollyItems within the Examples struct promotes consistency and scalability, allowing for seamless additions or modifications as the project evolves. Overall, this transition enhances code organization, readability, and flexibility, laying a solid foundation for future development iterations.

Let us now build an interface to display the data we get. Let’s create a new swiftUI file named DetailView to display the details of each item. To create the new file click on File → New → File… → SwiftUI File and name it DetailView.

We want our screen to look like this -

The DetailView currently looks like this -

Let us remove the default Text in the body. If we take a look at how our screen should look we will understand that we have all the elements arranged vertically. This means we will have to use a VStack.

var body: some View {
    VStack {
            
    }
}

Adding Item Image to DetailView

The first element we see is an image. Let us first import all the images that we will need for this app to our Assets.xcassets folder. To do this you will have download this compressed folder and uncompress it.

WollyItemImages

Once you have the uncompressed folder, follow the steps below to add it to the Assets.xcassets folder.

  1. Click on File → Show in Finder. This will open the following window -

  2.  Open the Assets.xcassets folder and add the uncompressed WollyItemImages folder in it.

  3. Open the Assets folder on the editor and you should be able to view all the imported images.

Now that we have imported the required images, let us add an image to the VStack.

var item: WollyItem
var body: some View {
    VStack {
        Image(item.title)
	  }
}

We will create a property named item of the type WollyItem and add an Image within the VStack. The image needs the name of the image to display it. If we take a look at the Images in our Assets folder, the image names are the same as the item title. So we will pass in the item title as the image name.

<aside> ❗ The preview will fail to build throwing Missing argument for parameter 'item' in call error. To resolve this we have to pass in any WollyItem in the preview.

#Preview {
    DetailView(item: Examples.muffin)
}

</aside>

The screen will look like this now -

If we look at our goal, we can see that the image is smaller and the entire image is visible. To do this we can make use of modifiers. In our case let’s create a custom modifier called fillImage(). This modifier is designed to ensure that the image fills its container while maintaining its aspect ratio and clipping any overflow.

Let us create a swift file named FillImage. To do this click on File → New → File… → Swift file and name it FillImage.
We will then create the extension function for Image.

import Foundation
import SwiftUI

extension Image {
    func fillImage() -> some View {
        self
            .resizable()
            .aspectRatio(contentMode: .fill)
            .frame(height: 300)
            .clipped()
    }
}
  • The fillImage() modifier is defined as an extension method on SwiftUI's Image view.
  • Within the fillImage() modifier, the image is configured to be resizable and to maintain its aspect ratio using the .aspectRatio(contentMode: .fill) modifier. This ensures that the image fills its container while preserving its original aspect ratio, preventing distortion.
  • The image is constrained to a fixed height of 300 points using the .frame(height: 300) modifier. This ensures that the image has a consistent size regardless of its intrinsic dimensions.
  • Finally, the .clipped() modifier is applied to clip any overflow of the image beyond its container's bounds. This prevents any parts of the image that extend beyond the specified height from being visible.

The FillImage file would look like this -

We will now add this custom modifier to our Image in DetailView.

Image(item.title)
		.fillImage()

The screen would now look like this -

Adding Item Title to DetailView

Now that we have added an image, let’s add the title to the screen. To do this let us add a Text to the VStack.

Text(item.title)
    .font(.system(
        .title,
        weight: .regular))
    .padding(.top, 4)
  • The Text view is initialized with the title of a WollyItem, retrieved from the title property of the item.
  • The .font() modifier is applied to specify the font style of the text. In this case, it sets the font size to .title and the font weight to .regular. This ensures that the text is displayed with a title-sized font and a regular weight, which is typically a standard weight for titles or headings.
  • The .padding() modifier adds padding to the top of the text, pushing it downward from its surrounding content. In this snippet, it applies a padding of 4 points from the top, creating space between the text and any content above it.

DetailView would now look like this -

Adding Item PriceTag to DetailView

When we take a look at the PriceTag we see that there are 2 subcomponents - a tag icon and the item price, arranged horizontally. We will use a HStack and add the two elements inside this.

HStack {
    Image(systemName: "tag.fill")
    Text(String(format: "$%.02f",
                item.price))
}
.foregroundColor(.white)
.font(.system(.title3,
              design: .monospaced,
              weight: .regular))
.padding(12)
.background {
    Capsule()
        .fill(.secondary)
}
  • Inside the HStack, an Image view is created with the system symbol "tag.fill", representing an icon. Alongside the image, a Text view is constructed to display the price of a WollyItem. The price is formatted using String(format: "$%.02f", item.price), which ensures that the price is displayed with a dollar sign, followed by the price value rounded to two decimal places.
  • The .foregroundColor() modifier sets the color of the entire HStack content to white, ensuring that both the image and text are displayed in white color. The .font() modifier is then applied to specify the font style of the content. In this case, it sets the font to system font of size .title3, with a monospaced design and regular weight. The monospaced design ensures that each character occupies the same width, which can be useful for aligning text in certain layouts.
  • The .padding() modifier adds padding around the content of the HStack, ensuring that there is space between the content and its surrounding views. Additionally, the .background() modifier is used to apply a background shape to the entire HStack. In this case, a capsule shape is created using the Capsule() view, and it is filled with a secondary color using the .fill() modifier.

The DetailView would now look like this -

Adding a Button to DetailView

Next let’s add a Button to add item to the shopping cart. We’ll also add a spacer to make sure the button stays at the bottom of the page.

Spacer()
Button("Add to Shopping List") {
    
}

Our screen would now look like this -

Let us style the button now. To do this let’s create a custom ButtonStyle named boldButtonStyle. To do this create a new file by clicking on File → New → File… → Swift file and name it as BoldButtonStyle. Then we will add the following code in it.

import SwiftUI

extension ButtonStyle where Self == BoldButtonStyle {
    static var boldButtonStyle: BoldButtonStyle { .init() }
}

struct BoldButtonStyle: ButtonStyle {
    @Environment(\\.isEnabled) var isEnabled;
    
    func makeBody(configuration: Configuration) -> some View {
        configuration.label
            .font(.system(.title2, design: .rounded, weight: .bold))
            .foregroundColor(.white)
            .frame(maxWidth: .infinity)
            .padding()
            .background {
                RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 12)
                    .fill(isEnabled ? Color.pink : Color.secondary)
                    .opacity(configuration.isPressed ? 0.6 : 1)
            }
            .padding(40)
    }
}
  • The code begins with an extension on ButtonStyle where the constraint ensures the extension is applied only to BoldButtonStyle. It introduces a static computed property boldButtonStyle which returns an instance of BoldButtonStyle. This static property enables easy access to the BoldButtonStyle without needing to manually initialize it.
  • The BoldButtonStyle struct conforms to the ButtonStyle protocol, which defines the appearance and interaction behavior of buttons in SwiftUI. Within this struct, an environment variable isEnabled is declared, which determines whether the button is enabled or disabled based on the context.
  • The ****makeBody Function is required by the ButtonStyle protocol and is used to define the appearance of the button. It takes a Configuration parameter, which provides information about the button's current state and allows customization of its appearance. In this function:
    • The label of the button is retrieved from the configuration and styled with a bold system font, white foreground color, and maximum width using .font(), .foregroundColor(), and .frame() modifiers respectively.
    • Padding is applied around the button's content to create spacing between the text and the button's border.
    • The button's background is defined using a RoundedRectangle shape with a corner radius of 12. The background color is determined by the isEnabled environment variable, with pink color for enabled state and secondary color for disabled state. Additionally, the opacity of the background is reduced when the button is pressed, creating a visual feedback effect.
  • Lastly, additional padding is applied around the entire button, ensuring adequate spacing between the button and its surrounding views.

The BoldButtonStyle file would look like this -

Next we will add this custom style to the Button in DetailView .

Button("Add to Shopping List") {
                
}
.buttonStyle(.boldButtonStyle)

Our screen would now look like this -

Modifications to ListRowView

In the previous droplet, the ListRowView looked like this -

And this is how our code looked -

import SwiftUI

let imageName: String
let title: String
let price: Double

var body: some View {

		    Image(systemName: imageName)
		        .foregroundColor(.pink)
		    Text(title)

#Preview {

Let’s create a property named item of the type WollyItem and remove the properties imageName, title and price. We will replace these properties wherever used by calling the values using item.

Our updated code would look like this -

#Preview {

Now that we have completed the design of the DetailView screen, let’s navigate to it from ContentView.

To do this, let’s modify the code present in the NavigationLink. In place of Text(DetailView) we will call the DetailView and pass in the item.

NavigationLink {
    DetailView(item: item)
}

Our code will now look like this -

Now that we have completed the navigation from ContentView to DetailView let’s work on adding items to the cart. To do this we will start by adding functionalities to buttons in ListRowView and DetailView to add items to the cart and create a CartView to display all the items in the cart.

Understanding State

In declarative UI frameworks like SwiftUI, views are a representation of their current states. States are the values of instance variables within a view's structure. By updating the state, you trigger updates in the corresponding views.

SwiftUI provides property wrappers like @State, @Binding, @ObservedObject, @Environment, and @StateObject to manage states in views. These property wrappers define how data is shared and updated within the SwiftUI view hierarchy.

It's crucial to maintain a single source of truth for the data in your application. This ensures consistency and avoids conflicts when managing and updating data across different views.

When passing data between views, use @Binding or @ObservedObject to refer to the source of truth when you need to make changes. These property wrappers establish a connection between views and their shared data, enabling bidirectional communication.

If you only need to display immutable data in a view without modifying it, you can use let to declare the data. This approach ensures that the data remains unchanged and reflects the current state of the application.

Modifying ListRowView

Let’s modify the item property by making use of the @Binding property. Let’s also add another property named cart with @Binding.

@Binding var item: WollyItem
@Binding var cart: [WollyItem]
  • @Binding var item: WollyItem represents the WollyItem displayed in the row. It allows external data to be passed into the view and enables changes made to the item within the view to be reflected elsewhere.
  • @Binding var cart: [WollyItem]represents the shopping cart containing WollyItem objects. Similar to the item binding, it enables changes made to the cart within the view to be reflected elsewhere.

Let’s also modify the #Preview section.

var cartPreviewListRowView = [WollyItem]()
#Preview {
    ListRowView(item: .constant(Examples.muffin),
                cart: .constant(cartPreviewListRowView))
}

This code sets up a preview for the ListRowView SwiftUI view, displaying a single row representing a product item. It uses a specific item (Examples.muffin) and an empty cart array (cartPreviewListRowView) for demonstration. This preview helps assess the appearance and functionality of the ListRowView component.

The code and screen should look like this once we do these modifications.

Modifying DetailView

Similarly to ListRowView let’s add the following code.

@Binding var item: WollyItem
@Binding var cart: [WollyItem]

Let’s update #Preview as well.

var cartPreviewDetailView = [WollyItem]()
#Preview {
    DetailView(item: .constant(Examples.muffin),
               cart: .constant(cartPreviewDetailView))

The code should now look like this -

Modifying ContentView

Let’s update the code in ContentView to this -

struct ContentView: View {
    @State private var cart = [WollyItem]()
    @State private var items = Examples.wollyItems
    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack {
            List($items) { $item in
                NavigationLink {
                    DetailView(item: $item, cart: $cart)
                } label: {
                    ListRowView(
                        item: $item,
                        cart: $cart)
                        .padding(.vertical, 8)
                }
            }
            .navigationTitle("Wolly's Mobile")
        }
        .accentColor(.pink)
    }
}
  • @State private var cart = [WollyItem]()represents the shopping cart, initialized as an empty array of WollyItem.
  • @State private var items = Examples.wollyItemsvariable holds the array of items fetched from Examples.wollyItems.
  • Each item in the list is wrapped in a NavigationLink, which navigates to the DetailView when tapped.
  • The label for each NavigationLink is a ListRowView, passing in the item and cart as bindings.

Creating CartView

Let’s create the CartView which will contain items that are present in the cart. Our goal is to create the following screens.

To do this, let’s start by creating a new SwiftUI file named CartView. Click on File → New → File… → SwiftUI file and name it as CartView. Let us also remove the default Text from the file.

Now let’s add the following code -

import SwiftUI

struct CartView: View {
    @Environment(\\.dismiss) var dismiss
    @Binding var cart: [WollyItem]
    let message = "Add items to your Shopping List to have them show up here."
    
    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack {
            VStack {
                if (cart.isEmpty) {
                    Text(message)
                        .font(.system(.body, design: .rounded))
                        .padding(40)
                        .multilineTextAlignment(.center)
                } else {
                    VStack {
                        List($cart, editActions: [.delete, .move]) {
                            ListRowView(item: $0, cart: $cart, addDisabled: true)
                        }
                        
                        Button("Clear Shopping List") {
                            withAnimation {
                                cart.removeAll()
                            }
                        }
                        .buttonStyle(.boldButtonStyle)
                        .padding(.top, 10)
                    }
                }
            }
            .navigationTitle("Shopping List")
            .navigationBarTitleDisplayMode(.inline)
            .toolbar {
                if (!cart.isEmpty) {
                    ToolbarItem(placement: .navigationBarLeading) {
                        EditButton()
                    }
                }
                ToolbarItem(placement: .navigationBarTrailing) {
                    Button("Close") {
                        dismiss()
                    }
                    
                }
            }
            .tint(.pink)
        }
    }
}

#Preview {
    CartView(cart: .constant(Examples.wollyItems))
}
  • @Environment(\\.dismiss) var dismiss accesses the environment value for dismissing the view. It allows the view to dismiss itself programmatically.
  • @Binding var cart: [WollyItem]represents the shopping cart, allowing external data changes to be reflected in the view.
  • let message = "Add items to your Shopping List to have them show up here.": This message is displayed when the cart is empty, informing the user to add items to view them.
  • The body of the view contains a NavigationStack, providing navigation functionality. Inside the stack, a VStack is used to arrange content vertically. If the cart is empty, the message is displayed using a Text view. Otherwise, a List displays the items in the cart, with edit actions for deleting and moving items. A button labeled "Clear Shopping List" allows the user to remove all items from the cart when tapped.
  • The toolbar contains leading and trailing items based on the cart's state. If the cart is not empty, an EditButton is displayed on the leading side for editing the cart. A "Close" button on the trailing side dismisses the CartView.
  • The tint color of the view is set to pink using the .tint() modifier
  • The CartView is previewed with sample cart data (Examples.wollyItems) using the #Preview block, allowing developers to visualize its appearance and behavior.

The CartView should look like this -

Adding functionality to add Item to Cart

Now let’s add the actions to the buttons in DetailView and ListRowView. Let’s start with DetailView. When the button is clicked, we want to add or append the item to the cart.

Button("Add to Shopping List") {
    cart.append(item)
}
.buttonStyle(.boldButtonStyle)

Let’s do the same in ListRowView as well.

Button {
    withAnimation() {
        cart.append(item)                    
    }
} label: {
    Text(String(format: "$%.02f", item.price))
        .font(.system(.body, design: .monospaced, weight: .regular))
}
.tint(.pink)
.buttonStyle(.bordered)
.disabled(addDisabled)

Navigating to CartView

To navigate to CartView from ContentView, let’s add an icon in ContentView. Let’s create a view where we show the cart icon with the number of items present in the cart. To do this let’s start by creating a new swiftUI file named CartButtonView.

Let’s add the following code -

import SwiftUI

struct CartButtonView: View {
    @Binding var cart: [WollyItem]
    
    var body: some View {
        ZStack(alignment: .bottomLeading) {
            Image(systemName: "cart")
                .padding(.bottom, 10)
                .padding(.leading, 4)
            
            if (cart.count > 0) {
                Text("\\(cart.count)")
                    .font(.system(.caption, design: .rounded, weight: .heavy))
                    .foregroundColor(Color.white)
                    .padding(6)
                    .background {
                        Circle().fill(Color.pink)
                    }
                    .transition(.scale)
            }
        }
    }
}

#Preview {
    CartButtonView(cart: .constant([WollyItem]()))
}
  • @Binding var cart: [WollyItem]represents the shopping cart, allowing external changes to be reflected in the view.
  • The body of the view contains a ZStack to overlay views on top of each other. Inside the stack, an Image view displays a shopping cart icon (systemName: "cart"). The icon is adjusted with padding to position it correctly within the button.
  • If the cart is not empty (cart.count > 0), a Text view displaying the count of items in the cart is overlaid on top of the shopping cart icon. The count is represented using the cart.count value. The text is styled with a heavy system font, white color, and rounded design. It's positioned with padding, with a pink background color inside a circle shape.
  • The appearance of the count text is animated using the .transition(.scale) modifier, providing a smooth scaling effect when it's added or removed.
  • The CartButtonView is previewed with an empty cart ([WollyItem]()) using the #Preview block, allowing developers to visualize its appearance in a preview environment.

The CartButtonView should look like this now -

Let’s now add this to the ContentView. We will first add a @State property named showCart and set it to false. Then we will add the toolbar item.

struct ContentView: View {
    @State private var cart = [WollyItem]()
    @State private var showCart = false
    @State private var items = Examples.wollyItems
    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack {
            List($items) { $item in
                NavigationLink {
                    DetailView(item: $item, cart: $cart)
                } label: {
                    ListRowView(
                        item: $item,
                        cart: $cart)
                        .padding(.vertical, 8)
                }
            }
            .navigationTitle("Wolly's Mobile")
            .toolbar {
                ToolbarItem(placement: .navigationBarTrailing) {
                    Button {
                        showCart = true
                    } label: {
                        CartButtonView(cart: $cart)
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        .accentColor(.pink)
    }
}
  • @State private var showCart = false variable controls the visibility of the cart view. It's initially set to false.
  • A toolbar item with a trailing placement contains a button. When tapped, it sets showCart to true.
  • The button in the toolbar contains a CartButtonView, displaying the shopping cart icon and the count of items in the cart.

The code now looks like this -

While the cart icon is displaying the number of items in cart we are yet to implement the navigation to the CartView. We will create a sheet to display CartView. To do this we will make the following changes in ContentView.

.accentColor(.pink)
.sheet(isPresented: $showCart) {
    CartView(cart: $cart)
}
  • .sheet(isPresented: $showCart) { CartView(cart: $cart) }presents a modal sheet when the showCart state variable is set to true.
  • isPresented: $showCartcontrols the visibility of the sheet. When showCart is true, the sheet is presented.
  • { CartView(cart: $cart) }closure defines the content of the sheet, which in this case is the CartView initialized with a binding to the cart state variable.

The code will now look like this -

We now have an app that is responsive, maintainable, and efficient in managing data and updating views across the entire application hierarchy.
